title: Config safety hypothesis testing for batching/cache rollforward
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Objective: Define and run a hypothesis-driven evaluation that quantifies the latency vs. quality risk surface when rolling forward batching/pack/TTL and KV-eviction parameter changes. The goal is to produce a safety gate for automated rollforwards that balances SLOs and LQ (latency-quality) regression risk and prescribes rollback thresholds and targeted canary slices.
experiment_plan:
1) Select representative workload slices (short-chat, long-context instruct, high-entropy Q&A, embeddings mix).
2) Choose config axes: microbatch size, prefix KV TTL, pack threshold, eviction policy (LRU vs age-based), token-aggregation window.
3) For each axis, run controlled A/B tests vs baseline across throughput targets (1x, 5x, 10x).
4) Measure latency P50/P90/P99, tail CPU/GPU utilization, token cost delta, and quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE for structured tasks, embedding cosine drift, and a proprietary LQ score for generation hallucination).
5) Use paired hypothesis testing (bootstrap CI) and per-slice significance to detect meaningful regressions.
6) Produce a ranked risk table and recommended gating rules (hard SLO thresholds + soft quality budgets).
results_snapshot: Preliminary runs (3 variants x 4 slices): median latency uplift 8-12% for aggressive packing; P99 increased 20% on long-context slice under 10x throughput. LQ_score delta: variant A ~+0.3% (within noise), variant B ~-2.4% on long-context (statistically significant, p<0.01). Embedding cosine shifts negligible (<0.2% overall). One config causes a higher error_rate for edge tokenization patterns (investigating).
observations: Aggressive microbatching reduces per-token cost by ~9% but increases tail latency for sequences >2048 tokens.
Prefix KV TTL reduction (shorter TTL) lowers memory pressure but increases cold-start quality regressions on repeated multi-turn prompts.
Age-based eviction yielded smoother latency tails compared to strict LRU at the cost of slightly higher token cost.
Quality regressions are slice-specific; global aggregates mask long-context failures.
decisions: Block automatic rollforward of 'aggressive packing' profile until targeted mitigation on long-context P99 is implemented.
Adopt a canary plan that includes explicit long-context slices and tokenization-edge slices when testing KV TTL changes.
Define rollback criteria: any config that causes LQ_score drop >1.5% on a customer-impacting slice or P99 latency regressions >15% on long-context will trigger rollback.
next_steps: Run expanded sweep across additional models (open-model-XL, redwood-turbo-1) to validate cross-model sensitivity.
Instrument new telemetry for tokenization-edge errors and link to failing request ids for replay.
Create a lightweight dashboard that visualizes slice-level LQ vs latency scatter with configurable thresholds.
Draft canary gating YAML to enforce the rollback criteria and submit for review (PR: github.com/redwood/infra/pull/1542).
